Retrieval Practice

Recall A1.2 (Data Representation) before we move on.

  1. Why is hexadecimal convenient when reading binary?
  2. What two factors determine an uncompressed image size?
  3. What is the purpose of a truth table?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

Why is hexadecimal convenient when reading binary?

Because 1 hex digit = 4 bits, so long binary strings become readable groups.

Answer 2

What two factors determine an uncompressed image size?

Resolution (number of pixels) and colour depth (bits per pixel).

Answer 3

What is the purpose of a truth table?

To list all possible inputs and the output(s), so we can verify a Boolean expression or circuit.

The Big Question

🤔 Your phone can stream music, download updates,

and respond to your touch… all at once.

How does one machine share limited resources fairly and safely?

❌ Misconception: "Apps talk to hardware directly."

If that were true, any app could overwrite memory, lock devices, or crash the system.

✅ Reality: the operating system (OS) is a resource manager.

It schedules CPU time, allocates memory, manages files/devices, and reacts to events via interrupts.

The Role of an Operating System

What does the OS do that individual programs cannot safely do alone?

Acts as an intermediary between applications/users and hardware.

Provides abstraction: apps don't need to know device details.

Enforces protection: processes are isolated from each other.

Core responsibilities

CPU/process management

Memory management (including virtual memory)

File + storage management

Device/I/O management via drivers

OS Functions (What gets managed?)

If resources are limited, what must the OS control?

CPU time (which process runs now?)

Memory (where does each process live?)

Storage + files (how is data organised and protected?)

Devices (printers, disks, network interfaces…)

Exam skill: link an OS feature to the problem it solves (e.g., virtual memory → running larger programs than RAM alone).

Memory Management

How can multiple programs run without overwriting each other's data?

Each process is given its own protected memory space.

The OS allocates and de-allocates RAM as programs start/stop.

Virtual memory extends available memory by using disk storage.

Press Down for a deeper look

Virtual Memory (What it is)

When RAM is full, some data is moved to disk (swap).

This allows larger programs / more programs to run.

Trade-off: disk is far slower than RAM.

So virtual memory increases capacity, but can reduce performance.

🧠 Quick Check

Why can heavy virtual memory use make a computer feel "slow"?

Because the system starts swapping data between RAM and disk; disk access has much higher latency, so processes stall.

File & Storage Management

How does an OS stop your files becoming an unsearchable "pile of bytes"?

Organises data using a hierarchical file system (folders/directories).

Provides operations: create, read, write, delete, rename, move.

Defragmentation can improve HDD performance by reducing fragmentation.

Note

Defragmentation mainly benefits HDDs (not SSDs in the same way).

SSDs have different performance characteristics and wear concerns.

Device & I/O Management

How can one OS support thousands of different hardware devices?

The OS uses device drivers to communicate with hardware.

It manages I/O using buffering, caching, and spooling.

Plug and Play

The OS detects devices and loads/configures the correct driver automatically.

CPU Scheduling

If many processes want the CPU, who goes next?

Scheduling chooses which process runs at each moment.

Different algorithms trade off fairness, throughput, and responsiveness.

Press Down for the main algorithms

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)

Idea: run processes in arrival order.

Strength: simple, low overhead.

Weakness: long jobs can delay short interactive tasks (poor responsiveness).

Round Robin

Idea: each process gets a fixed time slice (quantum).

Strength: good for interactive systems (fair sharing).

Weakness: too small a quantum increases context-switch overhead.

Priority Scheduling

Idea: higher-priority processes run first.

Risk: starvation — low-priority tasks may never run.

Fix: ageing (gradually increase waiting processes' priority).

🧠 Quick Check

Which scheduling approach typically gives better responsiveness for many users?

Round Robin — because each process gets a fair time slice, preventing one task from monopolising the CPU.

Interrupts vs Polling

How does the CPU react instantly to a keypress or network packet?

Interrupts notify the CPU when an event happens.

The CPU pauses current work, runs an interrupt handler, then resumes.

Polling means checking repeatedly: "Has anything happened yet?"

This can waste CPU time if events are rare.

Evaluating the trade-off

Interrupts: efficient for rare/unpredictable events; low wasted CPU cycles.

Polling: can be simpler and predictable, but may miss events between checks or waste cycles with frequent checks.

Quick Check

🧠 Quick Check

If a sensor updates once per hour, which approach is usually more efficient?

Interrupt-driven — polling would waste CPU time checking unnecessarily.

HL Multitasking, Resource Allocation & Deadlock

What happens when processes compete for resources that can't be shared?

Multitasking requires allocating CPU time, memory, files, and devices across processes.

A deadlock occurs when processes wait indefinitely for resources held by others.

Four conditions (classic)

Mutual exclusion

Hold and wait

No pre-emption

Circular wait

Prevention idea: break at least one condition (e.g., enforce resource ordering to prevent circular wait).

HL Control Systems

How can a system keep a variable "near a target" despite disturbances?

A control system uses feedback to reduce the gap between actual state and a target state (setpoint).

This is the same core idea behind thermostats, autopilot, robotics, and industrial automation.

Press Down for the loop components

1) Sensors → Actual State

Sensors measure the environment (temperature, moisture, distance…).

They provide a signal representing the actual state.

2) Controller → Decision

The controller compares actual vs setpoint to compute an error signal.

It applies logic/algorithm (e.g., threshold logic or PID) to decide an action.

3) Actuators → Change the World

Actuators turn decisions into physical work (open a valve, apply brakes, move a motor).

Transducers is the broader category: devices converting energy forms.

🧠 Quick Check

In a thermostat system, which component measures the actual room temperature?

The sensor — it converts temperature into an electrical signal the controller can compare to the setpoint.

Real-World Examples (Closed Loop)

SystemSensorActuatorLoop Logic
Smart irrigationMoisture (hygrometer)Solenoid valveStop watering once threshold reached
Autonomous brakingRadar/LiDARHydraulics/ABSHigh-frequency feedback to reduce latency

Misconception Check

A. Virtual memory makes programs run faster because there is "more memory".

B. Priority scheduling can cause starvation.

C. Polling is always more efficient than interrupts.

D. A control system uses feedback to reduce error against a setpoint.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Virtual memory increases capacity but disk access is slower than RAM.

B: True. Low-priority tasks may wait indefinitely without mitigation.

C: False. Polling can waste CPU cycles when events are rare.

D: True. Feedback aims to minimise the error signal.

Key Takeaways

  • The OS manages resources and provides safe abstractions for applications.
  • Key functions include memory, files, and devices (via drivers).
  • Scheduling algorithms trade off fairness, throughput, and responsiveness.
  • Interrupts react to events efficiently; polling repeatedly checks.
  • HL Deadlock and control systems extend resource and feedback thinking.
